column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The article says that at the state's re-creation in 1899 the title was reduced from Maharaj Rana to Raj Rana, and that the title Maharaj Rana was conferred on him as a hereditary distinction on 1 January 1918; the entry calls him Maharaj Rana from 1899 to 1929. The title change is left out of the text. The entry's library is not mentioned in the article.
The article gives no year for the Privy Council's ruling in Lesa v Attorney-General, so none is printed.
The article spells the Maratha leader Raghuji Bhonsle and Raghoji I Bhonsle; the entry's Raghoji Bhonsle is used. The fortress wall at Mahal is given as '3km/5km long'; the figure is left out.

The entry says the town was settled by Windward Maroons after the peace of 1739; the article dates the town itself to the resettlement after the destruction of Crawford's Town in 1754. The text gives the article's account of the founding without contrasting it with 1739; the editor may wish to check the entry's wording. Population in 2018 (just over 2,500) and the present acting colonel left out as changing figures.

The article's 'his regiment fought under Tunney at the Battle of the Dunes' is left without the commander's name, which could not be confirmed. The article gives little on the Leeward Islands governorship beyond its years (1671–1672), so the entry's account of it is not expanded.
The Kipsigis are described in the text without reference to 'tribe', the article's word.

The article says later generations took the Composition book as proof of title for the heirs of those named, but that Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford, denied this in the 1630s. The entry says the lords received 'secure title to land under English law'. To avoid contradicting the entry, the question of title is left out of the text.
The article says the public doctors may have acted more as public health officers or coroners and that this role seems absent in the Greek state; left out for length.

The article gives his dates as 5 May 1864 – 1914; the entry's dates read '19th century'. The death year 1914 is left out of the text to keep the page consistent; the editor may wish to date the entry. The article spells the king both Dhanurjay Bhanja and Dhanurjaya Bhanja; the latter is used. The name Dharanidhar Melli (entry) is not in the article.
The article lists the areas as around Victoria, Saanich, Sooke, Nanaimo and Port Hardy; the entry has Fort Rupert. The place names are left out of the text.

SKIPPED: The article is about a different person: Major-General Edward Osborne Hewett (1835–1897), Royal Engineers officer and first Commandant of the Royal Military College of Canada, not Edward Hyde Hewett (1830–1891), naval officer and consul for the Bights of Benin and Biafra.
The article dates the Court of Appeal's decision both 2003 (lead) and 2002 (background); the entry says 2003. The year is left out of the text.

The entry says he was mortally wounded; the article says he was wounded and captured and then either starved himself to death or was murdered in custody by his own grandson. The cause of death is left out of the text. Left out: the article's claim that he encouraged his men to eat the Arabs they killed, which it qualifies itself ('cannibalism was probably not normal Azande practice') without a source given.

The article calls him Governor of Cape Coast or of the Gold Coast from 1830 to 1844; the entry calls him president of the council of merchants at Cape Coast. 'took charge ... as governor' follows the article without contradicting the entry.

The article's excerpt does not detail the Hudson valley or North Carolina settlements named in the entry, so they are not expanded. The article quotes a churchbook of Dreieichenhain giving 15,313 emigrants in 1709 (cited through Henry Z Jones, Jr.); left out beside the official 13,146 and the entry's 'about 13,000'.

The article's lead says the grant was to the Mohawk; the entry says the Six Nations. The text follows the proclamation's own wording (the Mohawks and others of the Five Nations). Acreage left out: the article gives some 550,000 acres granted of the land ceded, while Ridout's survey described the grant as 674,910 acres.

SKIPPED: The article has under 300 words and the entry's description already gives nearly all of it (the exchange system, the Toolesboro Mound Group and the Ogden-Fettie Site); what remains (a list of states with sites, the size of one mound) would not fill the sections without padding.

The article gives his term as British Resident of the Orange River Sovereignty as 1848 to 1852 (and 1846–1852 in the lead); the entry says he was removed from office after his defeat at Viervoet in 1851. The end of his term is left out of the text.

The entry says the journal was kept in 1923; the article gives the engagement as December 1923 to May 1924. The text gives no dates for the stay. The article says nothing of passages cut from the first edition and restored later (in the entry's description); not repeated. The article spells Maharajah; the entry's spelling Maharaja is used.

The founding date of about 1450, the Beaver Wars from 1609, the Revolution's split and the treaties of 1784 and 1794 are in the entry's description and are not repeated. Left out: the article's paragraphs on cannibalism and slavery (contested and already summarised in the description as adoption or enslavement of captives) and Diana Muir's disputed expansion thesis.

The article dates Ogiso Ere to 16–66 A.D. without a hedge; the dates are left out and the founding is given as traced to his time. Left out: the claim that the street is the second most visited attraction in Benin City (a ranking) and the name of the present secretary.
The article's account of Kurunmi's death and burial (his head taken to Adelu) and the succession of Abogunrin are left out for length.

The entry says Kutai accepted Dutch overlordship in 1844; the article dates the treaty to 1845. The text gives no year for it. The article gives the schooner's name as Young (or Yonge) Queen; Young Queen is used.

The article names the Lady Washington's captain as John Kendrick and then says Captain Hendrick was killed; the captain is not named here. The uncle (Kaʻeokulani in the entry, Kaeokulani in the article) is not named in the text; the entry already names him.

The entry says she served as queen mother to Mibambwe IV Rutarindwa after Rwabugiri's death in 1895; the article says she was chosen as his queen mother in 1889, when he was made co-regent. The text gives no date for her becoming queen mother. The article says she was buried beside her husband Kigeli V Rwabugiri, a slip for Kigeli IV; the burial beside him is not mentioned. Left out: the article's remark on a present-day head of state from the Bega clan.

The article says the Wolaita continued to be ruled by their own king until the rise of the Derg; this sits uneasily with the entry's annexation and is left out. The tens of thousands killed or enslaved (in the entry's description) are not in the article.

The entry's dates for the revolt (1858 to 1859) and its leader's name (Tanyus Shahin; Tanios Chahine in the article) are not repeated. The Ghassanid descent is given as the family's own tradition (trace their lineage). Left out: the article's list of living politicians and businessmen of the family.

The entry says the office was created in 1919; the article says the chiefs coined the title Kyabazinga in 1939, after the titles Chairman and President. No year is given for the title. The entry says the office was restored in 1995; the article says traditional institutions were restored in 1993 and Muloki re-crowned on 11 February 1995. Only the coronation date is given, and the five-year terms are not dated (the article: 1993 to 2000 and the 2014 election). The article's eight-year vacuum (2008 to 2014 is six years) is given as for years.

The article gives his accession as 11 June 1922 in its lead and as his father's death on 6 June 1922 in the body; the text says June 1922. The port of Navlakhi, Morbi's industry and the engineering college named after him (in the entry's description) are not in the article.
The article gives no figures on rents or evictions after the act and does not mention the Land Act of 1881 (in the entry's description).
The article dates Cummene Find's death to 668 or 669; left out for length. Áedán mac Gabráin (in the entry's description) is not named in the article.

The entry says English commissioners ruled largely in Rigby's favour in 1646; the article says the Puritan Parliament affirmed his title in 1647. The text gives no year. The article spells the river both Sagedahock and Sagadahock; Sagadahock is used.
The entry spells the title Mushikavamsa; the article Mushika-vamsha. The article says Nandana may be the Nannan of Tamil Sangam literature, but cannot say so with certainty; left out.

The article gives his paramount chieftainship both as 1908 to 1926 and as gazetted in 1913; no year is given for it. The article is written in a promotional tone (greatest ruler, most advanced government, won wars without bloodshed); those judgements are left out. The article spells the British officer who met him around 1890 Fredick Lugard; the meeting is left out rather than print an unconfirmed spelling.

The commission of 1962 is in the entry's description; the article's figure of 88% for union is the Somali Republic's claim and is left out. The named massacres (Garissa, Wagalla, Isiolo) are left out: the article gives no dates for them, and Wagalla is not part of the 1963-1967 war.
The entry spells the title Basorun; the article Bashorun. Basorun Gaa's crisis (in the entry's description) is not in the article.

The article is about the family rather than the office; it covers both closely enough for the entry. The article does not say the branches held their states until Indian independence (in the entry's description); not repeated.

The article dates a satyagraha marked by violent incidents, after which Pattani argued with Gandhi and Gandhi halted the movement, to 1923; this is left out as the year is doubtful. The entry speaks of the Council of India in London; the article says only that during the First World War he was part of 'England's Indian minister council'. Worded as 'the council for India in England'. Kathiawar is the entry's spelling; the article has Kathiavar Peninsula.

The article dates the conflict 1957 to 1962; the entry gives 1958-1961. The range is not printed. The article's South Sumatra section has a rebel group under Major Nawawi surrendering only in early 1962, after a peace agreement of December 1961; left out so as not to contradict the entry's 1961 end.

The article dates his appointment as Burhagohain to April 1782 (and his premiership 1782-1817); the entry gives 1784-1817. The start year is not printed. The article spells the city Guahati in one place and Guwahati in another; Guwahati used. The article does not tell his installing of Chandrakanta Singha, which the entry mentions.

The article is short and says almost nothing of his historical writing or the library, which the entry covers; this text gives his education, offices and later career. The article calls him Rajkumar; the entry says heir apparent (Maharaj Kumar); neither title is repeated here.

The article gives his reign as 1568-1607; the entry dates him to the 16th century only. The end year 1607 is not printed. The article says 'reinstalled the idols ... in 1575' and revived the Gundicha Yatra 'eight years after the installation'; kept as given.
The article speaks of 'weeks of violent disturbances known as the Montreal Riots' in the lead and of a two-day riot in the body; the two-day riot is given.

The article gives his dates as c. 1425 - after 1495; the entry gives only fl. 1468. Not printed. The article argues at length that there is no record of his knighthood (Shaw's Knights of England), against Tupper, Balleine and the Jersey Heritage Trust; the entry calls him Sir Richard. The point is left out; the only contemporary mention, the 1495 attainder, calls him 'late of London Knight'. The article spells his ally Philip and Philippe de Carteret, and the son-in-law Phillip; kept as given.

Short article (about 400 words); this text uses nearly all of it. The entry's 'passed under pressure from the British government' and 'opened most civil and military offices' are not in the article and are not repeated or contradicted.
The article's list of Maroon officers and its account of a recent leadership dispute (arrests, rival claimants) are left out as present-day matters of living people.

The article gives the battle of Shopian as 5 July (Gupta, Sufi, Sethi, Gulcharan Singh) or 3 July at Hirpur (Saraf), and the entry into Srinagar as 4 or 15 July; worded with the hedge. The entry's later loss of Kashmir after the First Anglo-Sikh War is not in the article and is not repeated.
The article does not mention the entry's family allowances or invalid benefits explicitly (it lists 'the disabled'); not contradicted.

The entry says the Solymi's language and origins are unknown; the article says modern scholars suggest they may have been related to the Luwian-speaking peoples of Bronze Age Anatolia and calls them autochthonous. The suggestion is left out; the text says only what Strabo and the inscriptions attest about the language. The entry uses the spelling Solymi, the article Solymoi; the entry's spelling is used. The article says the Solymoi founded Termessos; the entry says later tradition linked them to it. Worded as 'accounts make them the founders'.

The article dates Sunassura to fl. c. 1450 BC and the 15th century BC; the entry gives fl. c. 1400 BCE. No date is printed. The entry's spelling Sunassura is used; the article also gives Šunaššura and Tudḫaliya, written here Tudhaliya.

The article is long but rests heavily on newspaper profiles and one 2026 chapter; only points it states plainly are used, without naming the writers. Lawsuits, the dispute with the Coushatta and other present-day matters of living people are left out. The article misspells the governor's first name (Jean-Baptise) and the city (Tallahasse); the text gives him as Le Moyne de Bienville and the recognition as by authorities in Leon County (the article: the city of Tallahassee and Leon County). The article describes the band as one of several organisations of people identifying as Apalachee descendants; the wording here avoids asserting more.

The entry says he brought Aranuka and Kuria under his rule; the article says his grandfather Karotu was already first uea of Abemama, Kuria and Aranuka and that Tem Baiteke's 1863 expedition put down Kuria's refusal of tribute. The earlier history of the three islands is left out and the 1863 expedition told as the article tells it. Binatake is given as another son of Tea, as the article has him (son of Tea and Karotu), without calling him a full brother. The article does not say that Tem Baiteke used firearms from European traders to win the islands, as the entry has it; not contradicted.
The article says the town was converted into a military barracks and renamed Maroon Town after the war; the entry has 'later known as Maroon Town'. Not repeated.

The article gives the landing as 12 February 1733 O.S. and says the founding is celebrated on 1 February 1733 N.S., an inconsistency (a New Style date should be later); only 'February 1733' is printed.

The article contradicts the entry's dates (fl. 1285, conquest of Shewa in 1285): it says the History of the Walashma has him die in 1276 aged 120, that most historians place his death at 1275, with Cerulli dating Ali Baziyu's accession to 674 Hegira (1275-1276); that Dil-Marrah's marriage was '5 years before the Conquest of Shewa' (i.e. c. 1276); that the dynasty overthrew the Makhzumi dynasty of Ifat in 1280; and that the dynasty ruled 1187-1559. All of these dates were left out; only the October 1271 marriage is given. The entry's 1285 conquest date and fl. 1285 may need a second source.

The entry says 'The name survives as that of a barony'; the article says the three cantreds were promoted to baronies in the 1840s, superseding Upper Ossory, and quotes the 1846 Parliamentary Gazetteer that it had been 'a few years ago practically abolished'. I described the cantreds being counted as baronies without saying Upper Ossory ceased to be one; the entry's last sentence may need revising. The entry calls the 1541 chief 'Brian'; the article names him Barnaby Fitzpatrick (Brían Óg Mac Giolla Phádraig). Both forms are given. The entry says Upper Ossory is the 'northern part of the old kingdom of Osraige'; the article calls it 'a surviving remnant of the once larger kingdom of Ossory' and the northernmost part of the diocese. No conflict.

Left out the article's closing list of current clan mothers ('As of 24 August 2026'), the Oneida forms (laothuwisʌ́tslaˀ / kutiyanéshu) and the adoption of prisoners and the Creation Story, which the description already gives. Present tense for the living institution, past tense for historical diplomacy.
